title: Automated tactile sensing
bibliography: L. D. Harmon, International Journal of Robotics Research 1(2), 3–32, 1982.
read_scope: Publisher metadata and exposed footnotes; full article unavailable. Not treated as a full-text or abstract review.
finding: An early review establishing the historical depth of automated tactile sensing. No quantitative sensor result from this article is adopted here.
limitation: Published material reflects information acquired before January 1981; historical recommendations are not current component specifications.
plan_action: Use only as historical background. Set limb requirements from the actual contact tasks and acceptance tests, rather than invoking human-equivalence targets from an unread historical review.
novelty: Broad tactile sensing cannot be claimed as a new concept.
bibliographic_note: Publisher gives pages 3–32; Cheng bibliography/user transcription gives 3–31. DOI 10.1177/027836498200100201.

title: E-skin: From humanoids to humans
bibliography: R. Dahiya, Proceedings of the IEEE 107(2), 247–252, 2019.
read_scope: Accepted manuscript: introduction and sections comparing electronic-skin requirements, integration routes and flexible/printed electronics; not every concluding paragraph or cited work.
finding: The viewpoint contrasts conventional components on flexible substrates with printed and ultrathin electronics. More discrete functionality competes with conformability; requirements depend on the application.
limitation: A perspective article is not evidence that a particular printed film has acceptable fatigue life, manufacturing yield, cost or multimodal accuracy.
plan_action: Keep a small number of proven modalities in the first product. Put packaged electronics on mechanically supported islands; qualify the complete interconnect and cover. Track area, installed mass and repair time separately from sensor-element thickness.
novelty: Flexible multimodal skin and distributed electronics were already established research directions.
bibliographic_note: DOI 10.1109/JPROC.2018.2890729; repository manuscript is a primary author source.

title: Tactile sensing—From humans to humanoids
bibliography: R. S. Dahiya, G. Metta, M. Valle and G. Sandini, IEEE Transactions on Robotics 26(1), 1–20, 2010.
read_scope: Indexed author/project PDF excerpts: classification figure 2, section III physiology, encoding and regional sensing requirements. Direct PDF retrieval failed; author-uploaded proof excerpts also located.
finding: The review distinguishes cutaneous from joint/force sensing, fingertip arrays from large-area skin, and slowly adapting from rapidly adapting tactile channels. Receptor density and required temporal/spatial performance differ by body site.
limitation: Biological receptor counts and perceptual acuity do not directly specify electronic taxel pitch, ADC resolution or required robot bandwidth. This is a review, not validation of our sensor stack.
plan_action: Preserve held-contact state alongside onset/change events. Specify coarse arm/leg contact localization independently from fingertip dexterity; retain joint encoders and actuator feedback. Test a sustained load so baseline adaptation cannot erase a real contact.
novelty: Biomimetic layering and biological data reduction are prior art.
bibliographic_note: DOI 10.1109/TRO.2009.2033627; author proof: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220032969_Tactile_Sensing-From_Humans_to_Humanoids

title: Directions toward effective utilization of tactile skin: A review
bibliography: R. S. Dahiya et al., IEEE Sensors Journal 13(11), 4121–4138, 2013.
read_scope: Glasgow institutional abstract and bibliographic record; TUM institutional abstract. Full original text not read.
finding: The authors frame useful tactile skin as a system problem involving distributed coverage, simultaneous contacts, acquisition, calibration and real-time interpretation.
limitation: The abstract supplies no verified circuit values, experimental operating envelope or manufacturing economics.
plan_action: Keep an acceptance matrix spanning material, acquisition, communication, body coordinates and application. A working single taxel cannot close the multi-contact, coverage or latency requirements.
novelty: System-level integration, distributed control and calibration are longstanding research topics.
bibliographic_note: DOI 10.1109/JSEN.2013.2279056. TUM corroboration: https://portal.fis.tum.de/en/publications/directions-toward-effective-utilization-of-tactile-skin-a-review/

title: Proximity sensing in robot manipulator motion planning: System and implementation issues
bibliography: E. Cheung and V. J. Lumelsky, IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Automation 5(6), 740–751, 1989.
read_scope: Author-hosted manuscript: system architecture/local planning, approximately manuscript pages 2–4; author project page identifying the publication. Not all experiments.
finding: The tested infrared arrangement provides a roughly 10–15 cm obstacle-detection envelope around the arm and coordinates sensing with about 50 commanded positions per second. Motion is constrained by the sensed free envelope.
limitation: The collision-avoidance argument depends on coverage, robot velocities, sensor characteristics and control timing; it is not a guarantee for arbitrary robots or objects.
plan_action: Do not describe our pressure-only skin as detecting obstacles before touch. If proximity is added, validate every joint pose and object reflectance/angle against the actual stopping envelope and measured latency.
novelty: Distributed sensitive-arm obstacle avoidance predates the proposed product by decades.
bibliographic_note: Author source identifies this file with the 1989 publication despite its IEEE 88 filename; project page https://www.edcheung.com/job/sbr/sbr.html.

title: Sensitive skin
bibliography: V. J. Lumelsky, M. S. Shur and S. Wagner, IEEE Sensors Journal 1(1), 41–51, 2001.
read_scope: Original article via MIT teaching archive: introduction; hardware/device requirements and low-cost-process discussion, printed pp.46–47. Other portions not exhaustively read.
finding: The paper explicitly links local processing, simple sensing structures, fault tolerance, repairability and manufacture. It discusses rigid active islands joined by flexible interconnects and warns that large-area signal paths collect noise.
limitation: The manufacturing costs and forecasts are historical; they cannot be imported into a 2026 BOM. Proposed future millions-of-sensors systems are not demonstrated production yield.
plan_action: Keep analog runs short, digitize regionally, provide failed-channel reporting, and cost scrap/rework and replacement operations. Compare complete installed harnesses rather than copper mass alone.
novelty: Low-cost, fault-tolerant, distributed artificial skin is an old objective; differentiation must be measured in implementation.

title: Conformable, flexible, large-area networks of pressure and thermal sensors with organic transistor active matrixes
read_scope: Open primary main text, fabrication and pressure/thermal experiments, figures 1–5 captions; not supplementary data or independent replication.
finding: A 12×12 network with 4 mm pitch combines pressure and thermal layers. Net geometry permits 25% extension; larger extension breaks strut wiring. The reported 2, 000 cycles at 20% concern simplified gold test structures, not complete skin. Organic circuitry uses −20/−40 V biases.
limitation: The combined thermal demonstration and transistor protection do not establish long-term humidity, abrasion or joint-fatigue performance of a commercial laminate.
plan_action: Use the established layered idea with simpler low-voltage electronics, but test heat paths and full-assembly strain independently. Do not substitute conductor-coupon fatigue for connector, adhesive, sensor and wear-cover fatigue.
novelty: Pressure-plus-temperature laminated skin is explicit prior art from 2005.
bibliographic_note: DOI 10.1073/pnas.0502392102. Full paper read through the substantive main experiments; no claim to have visually inspected all images.

title: Artificial Skin in Robotics: A Comprehensive Interface for System-Environment Interaction
bibliography: M. Strohmayr, doctoral dissertation, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, 2012.
read_scope: Selected thesis text: design tradeoffs in chapter 3; chapter 4.1 test procedures, printed pp.152–159; conclusions. Not the complete 217-page PDF.
finding: The thesis separates sensitivity and collision protection and evaluates the sensor with its electronics. Its proposed testing includes static indentation, repeatability, dynamic impact, recovery and overload; filtering affects sensitivity and reaction time.
limitation: These proposed evaluation procedures are not a universal certification standard. The thesis itself identifies unresolved performance tradeoffs.
plan_action: Add controlled dynamic indentation with an independent load/time reference, overload recovery and identical deployed filter settings. The thin TPU wear film is not an impact-energy absorber. Measure seam and mounted-curvature behavior, not flat coupons alone.
novelty: Combining mechanical protection with sensing is established; a quantified thin, serviceable implementation can still differentiate.
bibliographic_note: KIT title above is fuller than Cheng’s shortened “Artificial skin for robots.” DOI 10.5445/IR/1000028782.

title: Conformable and scalable tactile sensor skin for curved surfaces
bibliography: Y. Ohmura, Y. Kuniyoshi and A. Nagakubo, ICRA 2006, 1348–1353.
read_scope: Original six-page article: abstract, requirements, sections III–IV and beginning of V, figure captions 1–10. Remaining experiment/conclusion paragraphs not exhaustively read.
finding: The implementation places 32 photo-reflector sensing elements and a microcontroller on a cut/fold flexible substrate. Optical emitters are time-shared to control power; local SMBus connects to an in-body ring network. Bus capacitance constrains scaling.
limitation: Address-space capacity is not simultaneous full-skin throughput. The reported bare-sheet mass excludes subsequently added foam and the complete installed network. Foldability does not imply repeated stretchability.
plan_action: Use a small panel family and controlled mechanical relief. Measure aggregate power at the actual scan duty cycle, installed mass, and complete-frame freshness at maximum node count. Retain compact local analog wiring and a robust regional digital link.
novelty: Local scanning, reduced wiring, conformable modules and cut-to-shape skin were demonstrated in 2006.

title: Development of the tactile sensor system of a human-interactive robot RI-MAN
bibliography: T. Mukai, M. Onishi, T. Odashima, S. Hirano and Z. Luo, IEEE Transactions on Robotics 24(2), 505–512, 2008.
read_scope: Indexed original first-page abstract/introduction from Georgia Tech repository. PDF download returned 403; main experiments not read.
finding: The original abstract reports an integrated soft areal tactile system on RI-MAN and a human-dummy lifting demonstration. No numerical sensor accuracy or robustness result from the full article is adopted here.
limitation: Demonstrating a complete robot handling a dummy does not isolate sensor contribution or validate the proposed resistive panel. Semiconductive-pressure-sensor construction described in other reviews is secondary evidence only.
plan_action: Use a supported, low-mass test object for initial arm/body contact experiments. Document independently what skin detection contributes, what robot actuation contributes, and what protection is provided mechanically.
novelty: Large-area soft robot skin for physical assistance is established prior art.
bibliographic_note: DOI 10.1109/TRO.2008.917006; publisher article 4458232. Related open chapters were not substituted for this original.

title: ARMAR-III: An integrated humanoid platform for sensory-motor control
bibliography: T. Asfour et al., IEEE-RAS Humanoid Robots, 2006, 169–175.
read_scope: Original article sections on arm sensing and artificial skin, pp.2–3 of PDF, and hierarchical architecture/figure 5. Not all platform experiments.
finding: Shoulder and arm skin is integrated through dedicated controllers into CAN, alongside separate joint-torque and wrist force/torque sensors. The architecture separates task planning, coordination and execution.
limitation: This platform paper does not provide a standalone production recipe or prove that coarse skin replaces accurate joint or wrist sensing.
plan_action: Expose timestamped contact, location, confidence and faults through a dedicated driver. Leave actuator regulation in the existing robot control layer; test timeout handling at every boundary.
novelty: CAN-connected local skin processing and whole-robot integration were already present in 2006.

title: Design of human symbiotic robot TWENDY-ONE
bibliography: H. Iwata and S. Sugano, ICRA 2009, 580–586.
read_scope: Author-institution publication record and abstract. Original seven-page article not accessed.
finding: The design combines passive arm mechanisms and mechanical softness in joints and skin, derived from a set of assistance-task requirements.
limitation: The abstract does not expose contact-force limits, hazard validation, individual skin accuracy or a component-level manufacturing cost.
plan_action: Specify service tasks before adding modalities. Verify joint range, friction, cable pull and sensor prestress on a limb fixture; sensing alone cannot make an otherwise stiff mechanism mechanically compliant.
novelty: Soft covering combined with passive joint mechanisms is prior art.
bibliographic_note: DOI 10.1109/ROBOT.2009.5152702. Related Japanese 2008 appearance-design paper is a distinct publication.

title: Humanoid robot which can lift a 30 kg box by whole body contact and tactile feedback
bibliography: Y. Ohmura and Y. Kuniyoshi, IROS 2007, 1136–1141.
read_scope: Author laboratory bibliography and publisher record link verified. Original article unavailable; secondary syndicated abstract seen but not used as verified experimental evidence.
finding: The article identity/title documents an early whole-body-contact and tactile-feedback claim. The 30 kg result is a title-level reported claim here, not an audited replication.
limitation: No verified gains, failure statistics, force distribution or safety conditions from the original are available in this review.
plan_action: Cite the precedent without importing its payload. For our proof, compare skin-enabled and disabled behavior on the same restrained, low-energy fixture with objective contact-detection and response metrics.
novelty: Whole-body tactile lifting is not a new application concept.
bibliographic_note: DOI 10.1109/IROS.2007.4399592; publisher https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/4399592 requires JavaScript verification.

title: Whole body haptics for augmented humanoid task capabilities
bibliography: Y. Kuniyoshi, Y. Ohmura and A. Nagakubo, Robotics Research, Springer Tracts in Advanced Robotics 66, 61–73.
read_scope: Publisher abstract, chapter metadata and references; subscription full chapter unavailable.
finding: The abstract reports whole-body tactile covering of an adult-size humanoid and contact-motion experiments including a 66 kg human dummy.
limitation: The abstract alone cannot validate the loading conditions, control robustness or economics. It cannot justify human-lifting demonstrations with a home-lab prototype.
plan_action: Keep the early demonstrator on arms and legs, with bounded low-load contact tasks and no human support. Explain the eventual application without implying its hardware/control validation is already complete.
novelty: Whole-body contact capability and human-like distributed haptics are established motivations.
bibliographic_note: Publisher citation/copyright says 2010; Cheng/user list says 2011 and lab bibliography also lists the 2011 book. Keep this edition/year discrepancy visible. DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-14743-2_6.

title: An embedded artificial skin for humanoid robots
bibliography: G. Cannata, M. Maggiali, G. Metta and G. Sandini, MFI 2008, 434–438.
read_scope: Entire substantive five-page original article, including architecture, transducer, microcontroller, experiments and conclusions; figure captions. Images not independently resolved.
finding: Twelve capacitive taxels per triangle use AD7147 conversion; up to 16 triangles/192 taxels connect through local buses to one MCU/CAN. A grounded deformable electrode enables contact from insulating objects and shielding. About 500 Hz averaged sensing trades spatial detail for speed; individual channels are slower.
limitation: The reported prototype is six triangles, with quantitative experiments ongoing. Three-to-five-millimeter foam differs from our thin laminate. Port count does not imply adaptive rerouting.
plan_action: Keep local aggregation and distinguish normal-force sensing from bare capacitive human-touch detection. If evaluating capacitive alternatives, include the full ground-electrode, dielectric and cover stack and measure both spatial detail and response time.
novelty: Modularity, local conversion, CAN aggregation and adaptive spatial resolution are prior art.
bibliographic_note: DOI 10.1109/MFI.2008.4648033. Extracted area/power units in early PDF are ambiguous; no power-density number is adopted.

title: Methods and technologies for the implementation of large-scale robot tactile sensors
bibliography: A. Schmitz et al., IEEE Transactions on Robotics 27(3), 389–400, 2011.
read_scope: Author-uploaded manuscript: sections I, III, V and VI-A–D, assembly figure captions. Not every hysteresis equation or grasping trial.
finding: The 16-bit CDC yielded 8 usable signal bits in that assembly. Drift adaptation freezes while touched. Probe geometry changes response, and some body configurations omit a top electrode and rely on a human ground plane.
limitation: The extracted drift pseudocode has an apparent missing minus sign versus its stated ±0.5 deadband; never copy it blindly. Published sensor performance does not transfer to our resistive laminate.
plan_action: Freeze baseline during contact; test slow ramps and sustained loads. Measure actual noise-limited resolution. Test plastic, metal and gloved contacts. Calibrate several probe diameters and mounted curvature rather than claiming pressure accuracy from one probe.
novelty: Cheap replaceable COTS-based skin with distributed buses and calibration is prior art.
bibliographic_note: DOI 10.1109/TRO.2011.2132930. Uploader is coauthor Marco Maggiali; original author-site URL currently 404.

title: A flexible and robust large scale capacitive tactile system for robots
bibliography: P. Maiolino, M. Maggiali, G. Cannata, G. Metta and L. Natale, IEEE Sensors Journal 13(10), 3910–3917, 2013.
read_scope: Author manuscript sections III–IV, integration text and experimental figure captions; most main text read, not supplementary data.
finding: The design uses clothing-industry 3D spacer fabric and removable covers. On the flat 2 mm dielectric prototype, 15 load cycles with one-minute rests gave a maximum 9.1 fF cycle difference at 28.6 kPa, roughly 5% of range. Pressure-insensitive reference capacitors compensate structural thermal drift; they are not surface thermometers. The reported acquisition operates at 25 Hz.
limitation: Ten-minute constant-displacement relaxation is not a constant-force creep or lifetime test. Neither its thickness nor performance transfers to a 1.5 mm 100 Hzresistive stack.
plan_action: Use this as a capacitive fallback benchmark, subject to full-stack comparison. Separate thermal-point sensing from pressure compensation. Test both constant-force and constant-displacement holds plus local heating while loaded.
novelty: Fabric-based, protected, serviceable robot skin predates this proposal.
bibliographic_note: DOI 10.1109/JSEN.2013.2258149. arXiv submission 2014 is an author copy of the 2013 article.

title: A new silicone structure for uSkin—A soft, distributed, digital 3-axis skin sensor and its integration on humanoid robot iCub
bibliography: T. P. Tomo et al., IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters 3(3), 2584–2591, 2018.
read_scope: Indexed primary accepted manuscript section III-A/B, tableI and figure 1–2 captions; direct repository PDF retrieval failed. Calibration/results not fully read.
finding: Sixteen magnetic 3-axis cells occupy 26×27×6.05 mm; approximately 1 mm mounting tape adds thickness. Bumps and air gaps reduce normal-to-shear mechanical coupling. A first soft-silicone attempt allowed magnets to attract each other.
limitation: Full assembly is thicker and more complex than a thin resistive film. Performance in motor magnetic fields, chosen cover adhesives and our limb geometry remains unverified.
plan_action: Reserve this modality for a shear-sensing variant. If evaluated, test magnetic interference with motors energized, overload, cross-axis coupling and mounting-tape creep; include every protective/mounting layer in thickness and cost.
novelty: Soft protected digital 3-axis skin is already demonstrated; simplified normal-contact coverage targets a different specification.
bibliographic_note: Use the accepted 2018 manuscript as the source; no unverified calibration accuracy or DOI is invented.

title: An adjustable force sensitive sensor with an electromagnet for a soft, distributed, digital 3-axis skin sensor
bibliography: A. C. Holgado et al., IROS 2018, 2582–2588.
read_scope: Author-institution abstract and publication identity; original full text not read.
finding: The prototype replaces a permanent magnet with an electromagnet so current can change force sensitivity in a soft magnetic sensor.
limitation: The abstract does not establish a mass-production cost or justify extra power, thermal coupling and calibration for approximate normal-pressure sensing.
plan_action: Exclude electromagnets from the baseline. Add them only if a specified force-range problem cannot be met passively and a measured benefit exceeds coil-power, heat and driver cost.
novelty: Electronically adjustable magnetic tactile sensitivity is prior art.

title: Tactile sensing in intelligent robotic manipulation—A review
bibliography: J. Tegin and J. Wikander, Industrial Robot 32(1), 64–70, 2005.
read_scope: Author-uploaded text: introduction, sections 5.2–5.7 and conclusions. KTH thesis reprint located but oversized PDF could not be retrieved.
finding: The review separates distributed contact sensing from intrinsic force/torque sensing. It discusses mechanical inversion through soft covers, FSR/capacitive drift and hysteresis, and the loss of contact-pattern information in few-wire analog schemes.
limitation: Its supplier listings and dimensions are historical. A single resultant force/position cannot identify an arbitrary set of simultaneous contacts.
plan_action: Preserve separate taxel identities for multi-contact limb sensing. Do not infer shear, friction, material hardness or accurate force from ordinal normal readings without additional measurement and a validated model.
novelty: Resistive arrays, capacitance sensing, local processing and few-wire tactile tradeoffs are established.
bibliographic_note: DOI 10.1108/01439910510573318; uploader identified as author Johan Tegin.

title: Sensitive manipulation: Manipulation through tactile feedback
bibliography: E. Torres-Jara and L. Natale, International Journal of Humanoid Robotics 15(1), 1850012, 2018.
read_scope: Author manuscript abstract/introduction, hardware figure 1 and sections 4.1.3–4.3, PDFpp.12–15. Not all experiments.
finding: Obrero combines compliant actuation with tactile strategies for acquiring and maintaining contact. The text explicitly notes missed contacts at unsensed joint regions and a lift/retry strategy when immediate slip sensing is inadequate.
limitation: Success depends on hand hardware, force control and exploration strategies absent from our coarse arm/leg panels. It does not show that simply adding taxels delivers dexterity.
plan_action: Include unsensed joint seams in coverage maps. Demonstrate one bounded contact-aware behavior and compare against a baseline, recording missed contacts; do not claim general slip detection or dexterous grasping.
novelty: Tactile-first manipulation and active contact exploration are prior art.
bibliographic_note: Accepted manuscript datedOctober 2017 for the 2018 publication.

title: High-density conformable tactile sensing glove
bibliography: T. Sagisaka et al., IEEE-RAS Humanoids 2011, 537–542.
read_scope: Author laboratory bibliography verified; original full text not accessed. Exact-paper syndicated abstract and a distinct 2012 JRSJarticle abstract were seen, and are not substituted for the original.
finding: An established high-density sensing-glove research line. Original-paper performance numbers are not independently verified in this record.
limitation: Bibliographic aggregators merge the 2011 conference and 2012 Japanese journal article. Their results must not be silently treated as the same document.
plan_action: For our arm/leg application, evaluate range-of-motion change, cable pull and pressure offsets with the covering installed. Tree/branch geometry is a useful candidate, but requires complete laminate fatigue testing.
novelty: High-density conformable sensing and joint-motion-aware routing are prior art, not a new conceptual claim.
bibliographic_note: DOI 10.1109/Humanoids.2011.6100898. Related primary 2012 paper: https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jrsj/30/7/30_30_711/_article/-char/en (DOI 10.7210/jrsj.30.711).

title: Development and applications of high-density tactile sensing glove
bibliography: T. Sagisaka, Y. Ohmura, A. Nagakubo, K. Ozaki and Y. Kuniyoshi, EuroHaptics 2012, LNCS 7282, 445–456.
read_scope: Publisher abstract and bibliographic record; subscription chapter not read in full.
finding: The abstract describes 1, 052 pressure sites per hand using 1 mm elements on FPC, and human experiments relating pressure distribution to external-force direction and exploratory behavior.
limitation: Correlation in a human-worn glove does not establish calibrated robot shear-force measurement, full-body fatigue or inexpensive manufacturing.
plan_action: Keep human-dexterity claims out of the limb-panel proof. If comparing density, state active area, sensor-element size and pitch separately, with installed mass and connectivity included.
novelty: Thousands of tactile channels with flexible routing were already demonstrated in human sensing equipment.
bibliographic_note: DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-31401-8_40. Different publication from[32].

title: Tactile object class and internal state recognition for mobile manipulation
bibliography: S. Chitta, M. Piccoli and J. Sturm, ICRA 2010, 2342–2348.
read_scope: Indexed author-hosted original conference PDF methods/results excerpts, especially tablesII–IV. Direct PDF retrieval timed out; later journal version was kept distinct.
finding: At 20 N probing, reported container-class accuracy is 93.9%, while internal-state accuracy varies substantially by container (water bottles 32.5%). Stronger probing improves one container result, illustrating task and stimulus dependence.
limitation: An overall recognition number cannot be transferred across object types or contact forces; high probing forces can damage objects. These are controlled gripper observations, not generic limb-skin intelligence.
plan_action: For any classifier, report per-class confusion matrices and separate test objects/sessions from training. Keep active exploratory-force tests outside the baseline ordinal-contact product unless actuator force is independently measured.
novelty: Tactile object/state classification is prior art; any claimed advantage needs a matched task benchmark.
bibliographic_note: DOI 10.1109/ROBOT.2010.5509923. Do not substitute chitta 10 tro.pdf journal expansion for this conference paper.

title: A simple tactile sensing foot for humanoid robot and active ground slope recognition
bibliography: K. Suwanratchatamanee, M. Matsumoto and S. Hashimoto, IEEE International Conference on Mechatronics, 2009, 1–6.
read_scope: Publisher abstract and introduction excerpt, not the complete sensor/control evaluation.
finding: The work uses a small set of thin force-sensitive resistors and active foot interaction to classify ground slope rather than requiring a dense whole-foot image.
limitation: A foot-slope demonstration does not validate arm/leg pressure sensing or balance stability. Its load paths and contact geometry differ from shell-mounted skin.
plan_action: Keep feet as a separate subsystem. Establish whether a future task needs contact presence, center of pressure, slope or detailed pressure distribution before selecting sensor count.
novelty: Task-specific sparse sensing and active haptic inference are established.

title: Design and experiment of the NAO humanoid robot’s plantar tactile sensor for surface classification
bibliography: Q. Yuan and J. Wang, ICISCE 2017, 931–935.
read_scope: Author-uploaded original: abstract, sections III–Vthrough classifier setup, diagrams/captions. Final result table and conclusion not exhaustively read.
finding: A 10×16 resistive array uses 400 samples/s acquisition, but the authors explicitly state 0.4 s per full image; a 20-site subset supports faster tracking. Classification aggregates multiple walking steps.
limitation: The text’s 360 total datasets versus 224 training+36 test is arithmetically inconsistent. The headline accuracy is not immediate response or demonstrated cross-robot generalization. Matrix bypass-current rejection is not established by the viewed block diagram.
plan_action: Publish ADC rate, per-taxel rate, full-frame rate, scan skew and reaction latency separately. Never borrow 400 Hz as a full-array benchmark. Retain independent sensing islands unless simultaneous-contact electrical crosstalk is experimentally bounded.
novelty: Low-cost resistive skin plus simple classification is prior art.
bibliographic_note: DOI 10.1109/ICISCE.2017.197. Uploader is coauthor Jianxiao Wang; no outreach performed.

title: An adaptive sensor foot for a bipedal and quadrupedal robot
bibliography: K. Fondahl et al., BioRob 2012; Cheng lists 270–275.
read_scope: DFKI institutional publication abstract and metadata. Original paper not read.
finding: The work concerns an adaptive foot mechanism and its sensor integration for different legged platforms, rather than simply applying a sensing film to an unchanged foot.
limitation: The abstract is insufficient to reproduce mechanics, control or load qualification. The institutional page’s pagination conflicts with Cheng’s bibliography.
plan_action: Do not roll feet into the limb-panel BOM. A foot version needs its own contact mechanics, abrasion, overload, water/soil and gait-interface requirements.
novelty: Adaptive sensorized feet are an established separate product/problem class.
bibliographic_note: DFKI displays 2780–2786 whereas Cheng and other citations show 270–275. Flag the discrepancy; do not silently choose unverified metadata.

title: A ZMP sensor for a biped robot
bibliography: M. Shimojo, T. Araki, A. Ming and M. Ishikawa, ICRA 2006, 1200–1205.
read_scope: Indexed author-hosted first-page abstract. Direct PDF retrieval 403; complete derivation and experiments not read.
finding: The abstract reports four wires, response within 1 ms, 0.2 g/cm²areal mass, and simultaneous total load and center-of-load position.
limitation: These are compressed aggregate outputs, not independent contact locations.0.2 g/cm²equals 2 kg/m²; “lightweight” must be compared using consistent units. No claim about general dynamic ZMP equivalence is adopted.
plan_action: Test observability before replacing arrays: two equal separated contacts and one central contact can share a centroid. Our multi-contact requirement needs independent sites or another demonstrated reconstruction method.
novelty: Extreme wire reduction with analog spatial aggregation is prior art; it trades away information.

title: High-speed pressure sensor grid for humanoid robot foot
bibliography: Y. Takahashi, K. Nishiwaki, S. Kagami, H. Mizoguchi and H. Inoue, IROS 2005, 3909–3914.
read_scope: Author-institution abstract and bibliographic record. Original six-page paper not accessed.
finding: The abstract reports a 32×32 matrix, 1 kHz sampling, 14-bit conversion and 0.6 mm force-sensitive rubber. It explicitly identifies bypass-current interference and a mitigation method.
limitation: The abstract cannot supply the exact mitigation circuit or demonstrate our laminate’s independence, accuracy or fatigue. ADC resolution is not mechanical force accuracy.
plan_action: Our 100 Hzbody panels should not be marketed as equivalent to high-speed sole sensing. Any cheaper shared resistive matrix must pass a multi-contact test including unselected-row leakage, not merely isolated single presses.
novelty: Dense, thin resistive tactile arrays and scanning-crosstalk remedies are well-established research.
